meta.subtitle: KPI storytelling engine. Accenture Innovation Challenge 2026
meta.dataset: Olist Brazilian E-Commerce (public, ~99k orders, ~41k free-text reviews)
meta.honesty_note: Every figure in this report is computed from the public dataset named above. There are no hand-tuned effect constants anywhere in the engine. Retrieved web context is labelled as context and is excluded from evidence scoring by design.

scope0_triage.reasoning: Weekly aov fell to 70.795 against a robust baseline of 138.027 (change -67.233). Detected by a isolated excursion of -6.20 sigma in a single week, with the worst week at -6.20 robust standard deviations. A sustained excursion is what separates a real movement from the isolated spikes that searching 86 periods produces by chance. Welch's t-test on the underlying records gives p=8.89e-03 with a 95% CI of [-115.100, -17.519].
scope0_triage.rule: isolated excursion of -6.20 sigma in a single week

scope1_decomposition.interpretation: The movement is mixed (56% rate, 1% mix). Both the customer composition and the within-segment experience moved; neither alone explains it.

scope1_segments.note: Tested 0 segments. At a naive alpha=0.05 threshold 0 would be called significant; after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control 0 survive. The difference is the number of findings that would have been noise reported as insight.

scope2_verdicts.hypothesis: Delivery performance degraded, and that degradation drove the satisfaction drop.

temporal.note: contemporaneous at lag 0 (r=0.829); both metrics are anchored to purchase week, so lag 0 is expected. Mechanism ordering, delivery before review, is structural and cross-correlation cannot add to it.

evidence.claim: Degradation is in the CARRIER leg, not the seller leg
evidence.detail: seller->carrier handoff moved only +1.65 days while total moved -1.03; the carrier leg accounts for -2.68 days (260% of the increase)
across 0 segments, the size of the on-time drop predicts the size of the satisfaction drop (r=0.000, p=1.00e+00). A coincidental association would not show this gradient.
evidence.source: per-state deltas, event vs baseline windows

scope2_verdicts.falsifiable_by: Segments with large on-time drops but NO satisfaction drop would break the dose-response. So would the degradation sitting in the seller handoff rather than the carrier leg.
scope2_verdicts.reasoning: On-time delivery fell 5.9% (91.8% -> 97.7%, p=1.54e-01) and average delivery time rose -1.0 days. Decomposing the journey, the seller-to-carrier handoff barely moved (+1.65d) while the carrier leg absorbed 260% of the increase. The bottleneck is in last-mile transit, not seller dispatch. Across 0 segments the magnitude of the delivery drop predicts the magnitude of the satisfaction drop (r=0.00, p=1.0e+00), the gradient a real cause produces.
caveats: contemporaneous at lag 0 (r=0.829); both metrics are anchored to purchase week, so lag 0 is expected. Mechanism ordering, delivery before review, is structural and cross-correlation cannot add to it.

scope2_verdicts.hypothesis: Customer free-text independently corroborates a delivery cause, and rules out others.

temporal.note: review text is written after delivery; ordering is structural

evidence.claim: Product quality complaints did NOT rise
evidence.detail: 2.7% -> 0.0% (0.00x) -- this competing explanation is not supported by customer text

evidence.claim: Wrong item received did NOT rise
evidence.detail: 2.2% -> 0.0% (0.00x) -- this competing explanation is not supported by customer text

evidence.claim: Missing / incomplete order did NOT rise
evidence.detail: 1.9% -> 3.1% (1.67x) -- this competing explanation is not supported by customer text

scope2_verdicts.falsifiable_by: If product-quality or wrong-item complaints had risen by a similar multiple, the text would not discriminate between causes and this verdict would collapse to 'customers were unhappy', which is not a root cause.
scope2_verdicts.reasoning: Delivery-delay complaints rose from 10.1% to 6.2% of reviews carrying text, a 0.62x lift (p=4.7e-01). Competing themes did not follow: Product quality complaints 0.00x, Wrong item received 0.00x, Missing / incomplete order 1.67x. Because the rise is confined to one theme rather than spread across all complaint types, the text discriminates between explanations instead of merely registering dissatisfaction, and rules out: Product quality complaints, Wrong item received.
caveats: Topic detection is lexicon-based over Portuguese review text; only 32/46 event-window orders carry free text, so text rates describe reviewers, not all customers.

scope2_verdicts.hypothesis: The movement is a measurement or collection artefact rather than a real change.

evidence.detail: 99.3% -> 100.0% of delivered orders carry a review (SHIFTED). A collapse in coverage would make the score a selection artefact.
40.3% -> 72.7% of orders carry review text (SHIFTED)

evidence.claim: No pipeline gap in key date fields
evidence.detail: largest null-rate shift is order_delivered_customer_date (0.01% -> 0.00%, p=0.952). A broken feed would show a step change here. Judged by significance AND a 5% materiality floor, so small-sample noise is not mistaken for a pipeline break.
evidence.source: null-rate comparison across event vs baseline windows

evidence.detail: delivered share 97.1% -> 95.7% (p=0.555)

scope2_verdicts.falsifiable_by: A step change in review coverage, free-text rate, null rates, or order-status mix coinciding with the event window would support the artefact hypothesis and invalidate the substantive findings.
scope2_verdicts.reasoning: Four independent integrity checks were run against the event window: review coverage, free-text rate, key-field null rates, and order-status mix. 1 of 4 flagged. The largest movement across all checks is 32.44%, which is within normal drift. The metric movement is therefore REAL and not an artefact of who was measured or how, which strengthens every substantive hypothesis below.

scope2_verdicts.hypothesis: An external demand spike overloaded fulfilment and caused the drop.

temporal.note: demand measured against the 8-week pre-event trend

evidence.claim: Volume vs GLOBAL baseline looks like a spike
evidence.detail: event weeks averaged 44 orders vs 1130 across all other weeks (0.04x). This comparison is MISLEADING: the baseline spans a growth period, so ordinary growth is misread as an event-driven surge.
evidence.source: olist_orders weekly volume, all non-event weeks

evidence.claim: Volume vs LOCAL trend shows no spike
evidence.detail: against the 8 weeks immediately preceding the event (nan orders/wk), event volume was 44 (nanx, p=1.000). Demand was already at this level before satisfaction fell and did not rise further.

Carnival interrupts normal commercial activity across Brazil. Road congestion rises and logistics/shipping firms run understaffed because large numbers of workers take leave, which is documented to cause delivery delays.  [Context only. Not measured in this dataset; raises a mechanism, does not establish one]

evidence.claim: Retrieved context: Brazilian last-mile logistics capacity constraints
evidence.detail: Brazilian e-commerce growth in this period outpaced last-mile delivery infrastructure, with carrier capacity repeatedly cited as the binding constraint on delivery reliability.  [Context only. Not measured in this dataset; raises a mechanism, does not establish one]

scope2_verdicts.falsifiable_by: Event-window volume significantly exceeding the 8-week pre-event trend would support the overload hypothesis. It does not.
scope2_verdicts.reasoning: The demand-overload explanation is NOT supported. Measured against the global baseline, event volume looks 0.04x elevated, but that baseline spans a growth period and the comparison is invalid. Against the 8 weeks immediately before the event, volume was nanx (p=1.000): demand was already at this level and did not rise as satisfaction fell. Fulfilment therefore degraded WITHOUT a demand trigger, which points to a capacity or carrier-side change rather than a volume shock.
caveats: Retrieved web context is not verifiable against this dataset and is excluded from the evidence score by design.

scope4_decision.headline: Aov moved significantly (-67.233), but the evidence cannot identify a single cause.
scope4_decision.narrative:
**What changed.** Weekly aov fell to 70.795 against a robust baseline of 138.027 (change -67.233). Detected by a isolated excursion of -6.20 sigma in a single week, with the worst week at -6.20 robust standard deviations. A sustained excursion is what separates a real movement from the isolated spikes that searching 86 periods produces by chance. Welch's t-test on the underlying records gives p=8.89e-03 with a 95% CI of [-115.100, -17.519].

**Why this is inconclusive.** No substantive cause family is supported by the evidence. The metric moved, but no investigated hypothesis clears its own evidence bar. The competing explanations are no hypothesis. Reporting the marginally higher-scoring one as 'the' cause would present a coin-flip as a finding.

**What would separate them.**

**Decision required:** approve a short follow-up analysis, or accept the movement without a cause.

telemetry.cost_note: Priced at 3.00 USD per million input tokens and 15.00 per million output tokens. With no model calls the cost of an investigation is compute only, and does not grow with the number of KPIs monitored.

methods.technique: Median / MAD robust baseline, +/-3 sigma control limits
methods.why: Median and MAD tolerate contamination, so a large anomaly cannot inflate the baseline it is measured against.
Detects a sustained level shift rather than a single spike.
Unequal variance and unequal sample sizes between the two windows.

methods.technique: Additive decomposition of a weighted mean
methods.why: Exact arithmetic. Separates a change in composition from a change in experience, with no model and no assumptions.

methods.technique: Per-segment Welch t-test with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control
methods.why: Scanning 27 segments at alpha 0.05 yields about 1.4 false positives by chance. FDR control stops noise being reported as insight.

methods.technique: Two-proportion z-test, Welch's t-test, percentile bootstrap
methods.why: Every reported effect carries an interval, so magnitude and uncertainty travel together.
Attributes delay to the carrier leg or the seller handoff, which names an owner rather than a symptom.

methods.technique: Lexicon match (built-in) or unsupervised term-frequency lift with FDR control (uploads)
methods.why: For an unknown file no word list is supplied, so a finding cannot be an artefact of vocabulary chosen in advance.

methods.technique: Web search, returned as cited context
methods.why: Holidays, strikes and competitor moves are genuinely absent from the warehouse. Retrieved context is never scored as evidence.

methods.technique: Linear regression of segment effect on segment exposure
methods.why: A real cause produces a gradient across segments; a coincidence does not.
Compares exposed against unexposed segments, and tests the assumption the method depends on rather than assuming it.
An aggregate can move while every segment moves the other way.

methods.technique: Weighted composite of four measured components, compared across cause families
methods.why: Weights order findings the data already produced. They cannot create one.
Deliberate. Sentences are assembled from measured quantities, so no figure in the story can be invented by a generator.

methods.technique: Power analysis for two-proportion and two-sample tests
methods.why: Turns a recommendation into a test with a sample size and a duration.

methods.statement: No quantitative value in this report is produced by a language model. Detection, decomposition, ranking, causal testing and experiment sizing are classical statistics, causal inference and exact arithmetic. A language model is used nowhere in the numeric path; the narrative is composed from computed values by template. Retrieved web context is labelled as context and excluded from evidence scoring.
